title: North Washington Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: North Washington well records show a 30-foot median depth. Compare yields, water levels, drilling costs and site risks before buying or building.
h1: North Washington well records: what buyers should check
intro_html:
A shallow well record is not necessarily a household water supply. Around North Washington, 67% of permitted wells are listed for monitoring, while 12% are domestic or household wells. That distinction matters when comparing depths, yields and construction costs.

These figures cover Colorado DWR permit records within 5 miles of North Washington, including nearby Twin Lakes, Welby and Sherrelwood. There are 11,217 records, with 5,387 recorded as constructed. Use the area statistics to orient your search, then narrow it to completed supply wells with a comparable use and aquifer.

sections.heading: Why North Washington’s shallow median needs context
sections.html:
Among 6,228 records reporting depth, the median is 30 feet, and the middle half runs from 20 to 45 feet. That is a useful starting range for comparing shallow drilling bids, not a reliable target depth for a new household well. Monitoring wells dominate the local permit mix and should not be treated as interchangeable with domestic supplies.

Overall, 91% of reported depths are under 100 feet, but the deepest record reaches 1,751 feet. Permits name Alluvial and Quaternary Alluvium aquifers, while many leave the source unnamed or broadly classified. Ask the driller which water-bearing formation the proposed well would target and compare nearby construction logs before accepting a depth allowance.

sections.heading: Reported output is strong, but supply-well comparisons matter
sections.html:
Only 209 records report pump yield. Within that group, the median is 33.0 gpm, with a middle-half range of 13.0–101.0 gpm. Those results suggest productive wells exist locally, but the small reporting group and mixed uses make that range a poor stand-alone promise for a residential lot.

The reported share under 1 gpm is 0%, while 4% fall in the 1–5 gpm range. That does not guarantee a proposed well will avoid low output. For an existing home, request a current pumping test that documents drawdown and recovery. Also check the permit: a well’s physical pumping capacity does not establish how much water you may legally use or where you may use it.

sections.heading: Water is often shallow; the decade figures do not show decline
sections.html:
The 283 records with static water levels show a median depth to water of 11 feet below ground. The middle half is 7–23 feet. Static level means the resting water surface inside the well, not the well’s total depth or the level it will maintain while pumping.

Median measured levels were 37 feet below ground in the 1960s, 11 feet in the 2010s and 9 feet in the 2020s. These figures do not suggest a dropping water table; the reported water is shallower in the later groups. They also are not a continuous record from the same wells. For a purchase, compare measurements from the actual well rather than assuming this area-wide pattern applies to the property.

sections.heading: A monitoring-heavy permit history around North Washington
sections.html:
Permit activity rose from 548 records in the 1980s to 2,011 in the 1990s. The 2010s account for 2,868 permits, and the 2020s contain 1,053, with the newest permit dated 2025. These are permit counts, not counts of new household wells. The 67% monitoring share is essential context when judging how much residential drilling has occurred nearby.

The most active driller-field entry is Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 3,846 records. Named entries also include Layne, Christensen Co. (Tormoehlen, David A.), with 236, and Ground Exploration Llc (Bender, Joseph T.), with 111. Treat these as historical record labels, not a current availability or licensing check. Verify who is qualified and available for the proposed supply-well work.

sections.heading: Budgeting beyond a shallow drilled hole
sections.html:
The supplied cost model uses Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock at $50–$70 per foot. Applied to the 30-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $1,500–$2,100. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $7,500–$14,100.

Do not treat that finished range as a property-specific quote. The depth benchmark comes from a monitoring-heavy dataset, and the proposed household supply may need a different completion. Ask for an itemized bid covering the target formation, depth allowance, casing, grout, pump equipment and connection route. Have the contractor explain how the price changes if usable water requires deeper drilling. Access and the distance to the house also belong in the site review.

sections.heading: North Washington water quality deserves a property-level check
sections.html:
Within about 10 miles, the mapped inventory contains 689 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 189 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites and 1 historic mine feature. These are screening flags, not proof that a particular well is contaminated. Sampling locations and cleanup sites do not all represent the same exposure, and a radius alone does not establish a groundwater connection.

Before buying, obtain well-specific laboratory results and review nearby environmental records to choose appropriate additional testing. Inspect the wellhead, casing and surface drainage. Shallow groundwater also warrants careful septic and foundation planning where those improvements are proposed. Confirm required separations and site suitability before fixing the building layout. A neighboring productive well cannot rule out low yield or unsuccessful drilling on the lot.

sections.heading: Before committing to a lot near Welby or Twin Lakes
sections.html:
Start with the parcel’s actual water arrangement: an existing permitted well, a proposed well or another available supply. Match any existing well to its DWR permit and construction record. Confirm that the authorized use fits the intended home and any outdoor demand; an exempt household-use permit is not blanket permission for irrigation.

Then compare completed supply wells near the parcel, including records toward Welby, Twin Lakes or Sherrelwood where relevant. Match aquifer and use, not just proximity. Make the purchase decision contingent on suitable water documentation, testing and a realistic construction plan. For a new build, settle the legal water supply before coordinating well placement, access, septic and the house footprint. Ask DWR whether the proposed use requires augmentation.

faq.q: How deep are wells in North Washington, Colorado?
faq.a: Reported depths within 5 miles have a median of 30 feet, with the middle half between 20 and 45 feet. However, 67% of local permits are for monitoring. A household well may need a different depth, so compare completed domestic wells in the target aquifer rather than using the overall median as a drilling specification.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in North Washington?
faq.a: The model uses $50–$70 per foot, putting the drilled hole at about $1,500–$2,100 at the 30-foot median depth. The modeled finished well is $7,500–$14,100 with pump, tank, trenching and electrical. Because monitoring wells heavily influence local depths, get a supply-well-specific bid before using that range as your construction budget.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in North Washington?
faq.a: The 209 records reporting pump yield have a median of 33.0 gpm and a middle-half range of 13.0–101.0 gpm. Those figures show local production potential, not guaranteed household supply. Request a current pumping test for an existing well and confirm its permitted use separately from its tested output.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in North Washington?
faq.a: Permit depth and yield cannot establish drinking-water safety. The surrounding inventory includes 689 PFAS sampling/contamination sites and 189 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites within about 10 miles, but proximity does not prove a well is affected. Obtain property-specific laboratory testing and use nearby environmental records to guide additional testing before relying on the water.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in North Washington?
faq.a: The reported decade medians do not show a decline: depth to water was 37 feet in the 1960s, 11 feet in the 2010s and 9 feet in the 2020s. Shallower measurements mean water is closer to the surface. However, these groups are not a same-well monitoring series, so they cannot establish a parcel-specific trend.
